title: The 'Happiness Crash': As Young Adult Happiness Drops, Two Groups Are Thriving
gist: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer argue that young adults face a 'happiness crash' — unhappiness among 20-35 year-olds doubled from 11% to 23% since 2000 — driven by screens crowding out real-world socializing, while married and religious young adults are largely spared (50% 'very happy' vs 16% for unmarried, secular peers). They warn that declining marriage and religious attendance leave isolated young people vulnerable to online radicalization.

insights.claim: Since 2000, the share of Americans aged 20 to 35 reporting unhappiness has more than doubled, from 11% to 23%, a 'happiness crash' hitting young adults hardest.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: A structural deterioration in young-adult wellbeing is a long-run headwind for family formation, consumption patterns and mental-health service demand.

insights.claim: Anxiety, depression and anti-social behavior are rising sharply among young people, and growing numbers hold catastrophic views of the world and report a lack of agency over their own lives.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Low perceived agency among young adults can depress risk-taking, career investment and household formation.
insights.locator: But the poisonous fruits of the digital revolution

insights.claim: Smartphones, social media, gaming, pornography and AI chatbots have crowded out face-to-face conversation and community life, effectively running an uncontrolled isolation experiment on the generation raised in the digital revolution.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Frames consumer tech, including AI companionship products, as a social-harm vector — a source of regulatory and reputational risk for platforms.
insights.quote: Smartphones and social media—not to mention gaming, pornography and AI chatbots—have crowded out face-to-face conversation

insights.claim: Weekly socializing among young men and women has fallen more than 50%, from 12 hours to 5 hours, while they average three hours per day on social media.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Time-use shift from in-person to screen-based activity underpins attention-economy revenues while eroding offline leisure and hospitality demand among young cohorts.
insights.quote: Socializing among young men and women is down more than 50%, from 12 hours to 5 hours per week.

insights.claim: Teen dating has been halved, and two-thirds of eligible young adults are not dating anyone seriously.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: A dating recession is a leading indicator of lower marriage and birth rates, feeding demographic decline.
insights.quote: Teen dating has been halved, and two-thirds of eligible young adults are not dating anyone seriously.

insights.claim: Research shows social contact is a biological necessity: Harlow's isolated rhesus monkeys became self-harming and withdrawn, and Cacioppo found lonely humans have elevated cortisol, impaired immunity, poor sleep and hypervigilance to social threats.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Grounds the loneliness crisis as a health issue with measurable physiological costs, not merely a lifestyle preference.

insights.so_what: Rising isolation has actuarial and healthcare-cost implications for insurers and public health systems.

themes.theme: Marriage and faith as protective factors

insights.claim: Per the General Social Survey, 50% of married, religious Americans aged 20 to 35 say they are 'very happy' versus just 16% of unmarried, secular peers — a threefold gap.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Identifies a sharp wellbeing divide along marriage and religiosity lines, relevant for segmenting young-adult consumer and policy outcomes.
insights.quote: 50% of married, religious Americans aged 20 to 35 describe themselves as “very happy,” compared with just 16% of their unmarried, secular peers

insights.claim: Marriage alone substantially boosts happiness (37% of married, secular young adults are very happy), but the combination of faith and marriage appears most powerful.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Suggests marriage is the larger single lever, with religion adding further protection.

insights.claim: Unhappiness mirrors the pattern: 31% of unmarried, secular young adults say they are 'not too happy' compared with only 7% of married, religious peers.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: The unmarried secular segment — a growing share of young adults — concentrates the distress.
insights.locator: The pattern for unhappiness is the mirror image

insights.claim: The authors concede the marriage/religion happiness link is not proven causal, since happier people may be likelier to marry and attend church, but still argue faith and family are among the strongest bulwarks against loneliness.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Selection effects mean policy pushing marriage or religion may not deliver the full observed happiness gap.
insights.quote: These figures don’t prove cause and effect—happier people may be likelier to marry and to go to church
insights.locator: The pattern for unhappiness is the mirror image

insights.claim: An IFS report, The Devout Difference, argues strong marriages and regular religious practice are 'signal sources of social solidarity' that are especially valuable in a technologically distracted, atomistic and economically unequal society.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Positions institutional membership as the key buffer against tech-driven isolation.

insights.claim: The share of Americans aged 20 to 35 who are married fell from 58% in the 1970s to just 30% today.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Halving of young-adult marriage drives delayed household formation, lower fertility and shifts in housing and consumer demand.
insights.quote: In the 1970s, 58% of Americans aged 20 to 35 were married; today, just 30% are.

insights.claim: The share of young adults who never attend religious services has more than doubled since the 1970s, from 17% to 39%.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Secularization removes a key source of community, compounding the isolation trend.
insights.locator: The tragedy—and a big reason so many

insights.claim: The institutions best able to supply social contact — marriage and church — are precisely the ones young adults are increasingly disconnected from, a major reason many are failing to find happiness.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Implies the wellbeing decline will persist unless family formation and religious participation recover.
insights.locator: The tragedy—and a big reason so many

insights.claim: The authors hope signs of religious renewal among Gen Z are real, citing a new Harris Poll finding that Gen Z is now more religious than any other generation.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: A possible counter-trend; if durable, could support a rebound in community participation and family formation.
insights.locator: People crave something bigger than themselves

insights.claim: Isolated, adrift young people are more vulnerable to 'counterfeit communities' online — radical movements of left and right, from socialism to antisemitism — that leave followers more isolated and hostile to fellow citizens.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Links the loneliness epidemic to rising political polarization and extremism, a source of policy volatility.
insights.quote: more vulnerable to the counterfeit communities that flourish online—radical movements of the left and the right
insights.locator: The cost of this disconnection isn’t only

insights.claim: Drawing on Eric Hoffer, the authors argue those most drawn to mass movements are lonely people lacking purpose, and that marriage and faith answer the craving for something bigger by demanding sacrifice and binding people to others.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Frames family and religious institutions as civic stabilizers against extremism.
insights.quote: “A mass movement attracts and holds a following,” Hoffer wrote, “not because it can satisfy the desire for self-advancement, but because it can satisfy the passion for self-renunciation.”

insights.claim: Without a revival of faith and family, the authors expect a rising tide of political radicalization that turns the crisis of connection into a matter of life and death for the nation.
insights.speaker: Brad Wilcox and Maria Baer
insights.so_what: Signals elevated long-run domestic political risk tied to demographic and social trends.
insights.quote: It is a rising tide of political radicalization
insights.locator: Because the alternative is not just more isolation
